one_liner: Single-file C# Brainfuck runner that turns the program into nested generic types for RyuJIT; 2.9x faster than kostya's C++ interpreter.
what_it_does: bf-staged.cs (about 250 lines, MIT, contributed by hez2010 in PR #511) reads a Brainfuck program at run time and builds one closed generic type per instruction sequence: AddPointer<Next>, SubData<Next>, Loop<Body,Next> and so on, all ref structs implementing a static abstract IOp.Run. It then calls Run on the outermost type through a delegate. It is a benchmark program, not a library: there is no API beyond Executable(text).Run(ref printer), and only the suite's Brainfuck subset (no ',' input) is handled.
how_it_is_fast: This is first Futamura-style staging (program specialization) done with the .NET type system. Type.MakeGenericType encodes the parsed program as a type, and the JIT compiles a separate specialized method body for each closed instantiation, so instruction dispatch, the switch on op kind and the walk over an op vector disappear; what remains is straight-line code with calls or inlined bodies chained by Next.Run tail calls. Tape access skips bounds checks (Unsafe.Add on a Span<byte>), and the suite-wide Directory.Build.props sets TieredCompilation=false, so every instantiation is compiled once at full optimisation. The C++ baseline pays a switch and a recursive vector<Op> walk for every instruction.
when_to_use: As a reference pattern for runtime specialization in .NET: a small DSL, rule or filter program known only at run time that executes many times (bench.b: 185 instructions run for 0.37 s; mandel.b: 11,451 instructions).
When you want interpreter-to-native speedups without writing IL, Reflection.Emit or expression trees: the code generator is about 50 lines of MakeGenericType calls.
Workloads where a few milliseconds of type construction and JIT inside the run are amortized; both suite programs run for 0.37-2.9 s including that cost.
Teaching or comparing staging across runtimes: the same suite has Scala (Staged) and Racket (Staged) variants of the identical task.
when_not_to_use: As evidence that C# beats C++ at the same work: the plain C# interpreter in the same table is slower than C++/g++ (bench.b 1.280 vs 1.097 s; mandel.b 15.576 vs 10.143 s), and no C++ JIT or staged variant was benchmarked.
Memory-tight or start-up-sensitive processes: 36.62 MiB base RSS against 3.38 MiB for the C++ interpreter, plus the .NET runtime start-up that the harness excludes from timing.
NativeAOT, trimmed or other no-JIT deployments: the whole technique depends on Type.MakeGenericType and reflection at run time; the suite builds it only with dotnet build for the JIT runtime.
Untrusted programs: the tape is read and written with Unsafe.Add and only the right edge is guarded, so moving left of cell 0 writes outside the array instead of throwing.
Short-lived programs that run once for microseconds: every distinct program costs type loading and JIT before the first instruction runs.

integration.form: source-drop (one C# file, brainfuck/bf-staged.cs, built by brainfuck-staged.csproj)
integration.dependencies: none beyond the .NET base class library
integration.min_toolchain: .NET 10 SDK as built (TargetFramework net10.0; README lists .NET 10.0.100, current Dockerfile SDK 10.0.302); uses static abstract interface members and 'allows ref struct' generic constraints
integration.platforms: any platform with the CoreCLR JIT; measured on x86-64 Linux only
integration.thread_safety: not documented; each Run builds its own tape and the Printer is passed by ref, so separate runs share nothing but the runtime's type cache

gotchas: Different algorithm from the baseline: brainfuck/README.md requires every implementation to interpret instructions one by one without squashing, and the maintainer (nuald, issue #485, 2024-03-20) says staged variants are 'not the reference implementations, and rather included just for testing purposes'; the C++ side is the reference interpreter, not a C++ JIT.
Tape semantics differ: C# uses byte cells that wrap at 256 and loops on != 0, C++ uses int cells and loops on > 0; both suite programs agree on output, but other Brainfuck programs may not.

AtNoRangeCheck's comment says the address 'has been guarded in AddPointer', but SubPointer never checks the left edge, so a program that steps below cell 0 silently corrupts managed memory (the C++ interpreter's size_t index would also go out of bounds there).

The JIT and type-construction cost is inside the timed region (xtime.rb times from the program's start message to its stop message), which counts against the staged row; .NET runtime start-up and the Hello World self-check are outside it for every language.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Among the staged rows of the same table it is the fastest and leanest (bench.b 0.373 s and 36.6 MiB against Scala (Staged) 0.409 s and 229.6 MiB and Racket (Staged) 0.885 s and 101.4 MiB; mandel.b 2.917 s against 7.118 s and 15.722 s), so pick it when your host language is C#. If you must stay in C++, the catalogued ClangJIT and Proteus entries give C++ the same run-time specialization through LLVM.
verified_claims_summary: In kostya/benchmarks (README update 2026-07-19, Intel Xeon E-2324G, medians of repeated runs), the staged C# runner on .NET 10.0.100 with TieredCompilation=false ran bench.b in 0.373 s, 14.33 J, against 1.097 s and 46.21 J for the C++ AST interpreter built with g++ 16.1.0 -O3 -march=native -flto=auto (C/gcc 1.112 s, C++/clang++ 22.1.8 with libc++ 1.167 s), about 2.9x (derived from page data); the same pair runs mandel.b in 2.917 s against 10.143 s (about 3.5x, derived from page data). The win is run-time compilation of the Brainfuck program set against a reference interpreter, not .NET code generation beating g++ at equal work.
status_note: The suite is active (MIT, 2.9k stars, last update 2026-07-19), and bf-staged.cs has had exactly one commit (e645c23, PR #511, 2025-11-17); it is a copyable teaching sample of .NET generic staging rather than a maintained library.
